item.title: Building k9s for Linode With Bubble Tea
item.description: A lot of my day is spent in k9s, and when I need something from the Linode side of the house (a node that won’t boot, a volume nobody cleaned up, the kubeconfig for a cluster I just made) I’m back in a browser tab or typing linode-cli incantations. I wanted the k9s workflow for the Linode API itself: : to jump to a resource type, / to filter, single-key actions on the selected row, and Enter to go deeper. That turned into linode-tui, a Go TUI built on Bubble Tea, linodego and urfave/cli v3.

item.title: Stop Ctrl-C-ing Your tail -f | grep
item.description: Here’s a loop I end up in all the time: tail -f app.log, something scrolls by that looks wrong, Ctrl-C, tail -f app.log | grep ERROR, wait for it to happen again, decide I also want to drop the health checks, Ctrl-C, | grep -v healthz, wait again. Every filter tweak throws away the stream and every line that already went past. I got tired of it and wrote tail-gunner, a tail replacement that you can promote into a filtering TUI with one keystroke and drop back out of without the stream ever stopping.

item.title: Maintaining a Go Tool That Edits /etc/hosts on Every OS
item.description: Editing the hosts file sounds like the most boring problem in software. Read a text file, add a line, write it back. Then you find out your binary is being shelled out to from a Ruby Vagrant plugin on a Windows laptop with UAC prompts, your library is being called in a loop by ddev, and every hosts file you parse was hand-edited by somebody at some point. I’ve been maintaining goodhosts for a few years now, and since I just spent a chunk of the fall and the holidays on it, here’s what that looks like.

item.title: Practical Cue Example, Produce YAML Config from Go Types
item.description: I recently had to spend some time to learn Cue and felt the examples/tutorials were a bit lacking and the paradigm shift to the entire language sort of messed with my head and some things Cue does were a bit foreign to me. To get started, note that the two places I spent all of my time to get this information came from their main docs and a community Cuetorials site. This will be a tutorial on how you can use Cue to generate two different YAML documents using Cue all starting with Go types to generate Cue files.

item.title: Free Blog Hosting Using Hugo + Github Pages
item.description:
Since I just rode this merry-go-round here is a quick overview of how you can achieve a professional looking personal blog with custom DNS with minimal effort at no cost and completely run out of a single Github Repository.

Prerequisites

You’ll need to do your own homework on how to use Hugo and you should have a Github account and have a decent understanding of using git and getting changes committed and pushed to a repo. You should also have a domain and know how to do some basic DNS changes. Note that the only thing you likely can’t get for free is a domain name as there are registration costs through registrars but, you can get introductory $0.99USD domains for the first year if you shop around and don’t care the TLD you end up with. For reference, luth.io cost me $30/year to register with CloudFlare.
